TENTATIVE RULINGS FOR March 30, 2026

BEFORE THE HONORABLE TONY RAPHAEL
(909) 285-3717
ATTENTION: Commencing December 10, 2022, the Court will no longer
regularly provide an official Court Reporter to transcribe proceedings in this
Department. Parties who wish to have an official record of the proceedings in addition
to a minute order must retain a private Certified Shorthand Reporter for the hearing and
must submit a “Stipulation and Order For Appointment of Official Reporter Pro
Tempore” to the court in the form found on the Court’s website. If counsel are appearing
for the hearing remotely, the Stipulation can be emailed to the Judicial Assistant for
Department R-14 at SScott@sb-court.org. The Court may sign the Order appointing the
Certified Shorthand Reporter as the official Court Reporter Pro Tempore. Parties who
do not retain a Certified Shorthand Reporter to be designated as an official Court
Reporter Pro Tempore are deemed to have waived an official Court Reporter for the
proceeding.

PLEASE REFER TO THE GENERAL ORDERS AND FORMS POSTED ON THE
COURT’S WEBSITE.

PLEASE NOTE: There may be multiple tentative rulings so view the entire
document.

This Court follows California Rules of Court, rule 3.1308(b) for tentative rulings. (See
San Bernardino Superior Court Local Emergency Rule 8.) Tentative rulings are posted
on the court’s website after 3:00 p.m. the day before the hearing at https://www.sb-
court.org/divisions/civil/civil-tentative-rulings.
You may appear in person or by remote appearance at the hearing. (See www.sb-
court.org/general-information/remote-access ) If you do not have Internet access you
may obtain the tentative ruling by calling the department at 909-285-3717. If you (or
both parties) wish to submit on the Tentative, notify the other party and call the
department by 4:00 p.m. the day before and your appearance may be excused unless
the Court orders you to appear.

You must appear at the hearing if you are so directed by the court in the tentative ruling
and be prepared to address those issues set forth by the court in its ruling.
UNLESS OTHERWISE NOTED, THE PREVAILING PARTY IS TO GIVE NOTICE OF

RULING
Marisol Traconis
v.
1st Stryke Pest & Termite Control, et al.

CIVSB2126550

RELEVANT PROCEDURAL/FACTUAL BACKGROUND
I. Complaint and Answer
Plaintiff Marisol Traconis initiated this action on September 14, 2021, by filing a
Complaint against Defendants 1st Stryke Pest & Termite Control (“1st Stryke”), Leticia Ceballos
(“Ms. Ceballos”) and Does 1-25 (collectively, “Defendants”), alleging four causes of action: (1)
Negligence [against all Defendants]; (2) Breach of Implied Warrant of Habitability [against Ms.
Ceballos/Does 11-25]; (3) Private Nuisance [against Ms. Ceballos/Does 11-25] and (4) Breach of
Implied Covenant of Peaceful and Quiet Enjoyment [against Ms. Ceballos/Does 11-25].
Plaintiff alleges as follows. On October 1, 2019, she entered into a rental agreement with
Ms. Ceballos as to real property located at 416 ½ S. Fern Avenue in Ontario, California (the
“Property”). After moving into the rental Property, she discovered pests inside and reported the
issue to Ms. Ceballos. On October 8, 2019, 1st Stryke sent an employee out to spray for pests. She
was advised to leave the premises for four hours and return later when it was considered “safe.”
Plaintiff left the Property with her dog. Then, on October 15, 2019, 1st Stryke returned and
performed another treatment for pests. After Defendant treated the Property for pests, Plaintiff
began to feel ill. Plaintiff’s dog also became noticeably sick and subsequently passed away.
Plaintiff was hospitalized from October 23, 2019, to November 5, 2019, for organophosphate
poisoning, which was the result of Defendant’s negligent fumigation of the Property. (Compl., at
¶¶ 3, 10, 16, 17.)
On May 3, 2022, Defendant 1st Stryke filed an Answer to Plaintiff’s Complaint.
On May 13, 2022, Defendant Ms. Ceballos filed an Answer to Plaintiff’s Complaint.
II. Cross-Complaint and Answer
After the Court granted Defendant Ms. Ceballo’s Motion for Leave to file a Cross-
Complaint on November 24, 2025, she filed a Cross-Complaint against 1st Stryke. Ms. Ceballo
alleges two causes of action: (1) Indemnity, and (2) Contribution.
On December 16, 2025, Defendant 1st Stryke filed an Answer to Ms. Ceballo’s Cross-
Complaint.

III. Prior Motion to Bifurcate Trial
On July 30, 2025, the Court denied Defendant Ms. Ceballos’ Motion to Bifurcate.
IV. Instant Motion
Now at issue before the Court is Defendant 1st Stryke’s Motion to Bifurcate Trial. 1st
Stryke seeks to bifurcate the issues of liability and damages pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure
sections 598 and 1048, subdivision (b).

Plaintiff opposes the motion. 1st Stryke replies to the opposition.

DISCUSSION
V. Statement of the Law
Whether to grant or deny a motion to bifurcate rests within the trial court’s sound
discretion. (Grappo v. Coventry Fin. Corp. (1991) 235 Cal.App.3d 496, 504; Regents of University
of California v. Sheily (2004) 122 Cal.App.4th 824, 833.) “‘[A] court abuses its discretion when
its rulings fall “outside the bounds of reason.”’ [Citations.]” (People v. Franklin (2016) 248
Cal.App.4th 938, 952.)
Code of Civil Procedure section 598 provides in relevant part that:
The court may, when the convenience of witnesses, the ends of justice, or the
economy and efficiency of handling the litigation would be promoted thereby, on
motion of a party, after notice and hearing, make an order, no later than the close
of pretrial conference in cases in which such pretrial conference is to be held, or, in
other cases, no later than 30 days before the trial date, that the trial of any issue
or any part thereof shall precede the trial of any other issue or any part thereof
in the case, except for special defenses which may be tried first pursuant to Sections
597 and 597.5. The court, on its own motion, may make such an order at any time.
(Emphasis added.)
Code of Civil Procedure section 1048, subdivision (b), provides that:
The court, in furtherance of convenience or to avoid prejudice, or when separate
trials will be conducive to expedition and economy, may order a separate trial of
any cause of action, including a cause of action asserted in a cross-complaint, or
of any separate issue or of any number of causes of action or issues, preserving
the right of trial by jury required by the Constitution or a statute of this state or of
the United States.
(Emphasis added.)
“The major objective of bifurcated trials is to expedite and simplify the presentation of
evidence.” (Foreman & Clark Corp. v. Fallon (1971) 3 Cal.3d 875, 888 (“Foreman & Clark
Corp.”).) Factors to be considered in ruling on a motion to bifurcate are whether it will: (1) further
the convenience of parties and witnesses, (2) avoid prejudice, (3) encourage expedition, (4)
promote economy, or (5) serve the ends of justice. (Code Civ. Proc., §§ 1048, subd. (b), 598.)
Where the parties dispute both liability and damages, the purpose of bifurcation is to avoid
the time and money spent in trying the issue of damages when the verdict is against liability.
(Horton v. Jones (1972) 26 Cal.App.3d 952, 955; Estate of Young (2008) 160 Cal.App.4th 62, 90.)
VI. Procedural Concern
In her opposition, Plaintiff argues that Defendant 1st Stryke’s motion pursuant to Section
598 is untimely. In the reply, Defendant 1st Stryke relies on the Trial Readiness Conference
scheduled for April 2, 2026, and contends that the motion is timely because it was filed on March
5, 2026, more than 30 days before trial.

The motion is untimely under Section 598 because there is no pretrial conference being
held in this case and the hearing is less than 30 days before trial. (Code Civ. Proc., § 598.) A Trial
Readiness Conference is meant to confirm all preparations for trial itself are complete and to ensure
it proceeds efficiently. The hearing date for this motion is March 30, 2026, which is only seven
calendar days before the jury trial on April 6, 2026.
Nonetheless, the Court considers the merits of the motion. 1st Strike also cites Section
1048, which does not have a deadline for bringing such a motion. The question is whether
bifurcation is in furtherance of convenience or to avoid prejudice or when separate trials will be
conducive to expedition and economy. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1048, subd. (b).)
VII. Parties’ Arguments
Defendant 1st Stryke moves to bifurcate the trial so that the issue of its liability is tried first
and the issue of damages is tried (if necessary at all) second. 1st Stryke denies any allegation that
its products contained organophosphate. (Declaration of Cecilia D. Torello, Esq., at ¶¶ 5, 7.) For
the liability phase, it intends to introduce evidence regarding the condition of the property, the pest
control service, and Plaintiff’s hospitalization. Testimony is anticipated by Plaintiff, Defendant
Ms. Ceballos, owner of and pest control technician who performed the service on behalf of 1st
Stryke, five of Plaintiff’s family members, the City’s inspector, and eight experts. Each party will
call an expert toxicologist and a pest control expert; Ms. Ceballos will also call a property
management expert and 1st Stryke will also call an expert industrial hygienist. Plaintiff’s counsel
estimates that a liability phase trial would last three to five days, while a damages only phase would
last at least one to two weeks based on the number of witnesses. (See Torello, Decl., at ¶¶ 8-10.)1
Defendant 1st Stryke contends that if it prevails in the initial liability phase, the need for
the second phase of trial would be eliminated. 1st Stryke argues that trying liability first promotes
efficiency and conserves resources for both the Court and the parties. If it does not prevail, then it
would narrow the case and sharpen the issues for any subsequent damages presentation, reducing
trial length and complexity. 1st Stryke states it may have an incentive to settle before proceeding
to the damages portion of trial, thus reducing the costs for all parties involved.
Defendant 1st Stryke also argues that the claims asserted against Ms. Ceballos are based
on entirely different legal theories and states trying all claims together would unnecessarily
complicate the proceedings and increase the likelihood of jury confusion. It further states that
separate phases will enable a jury to address the distinct issues in an orderly and comprehensible
manner.

Defendant 1st Stryke likewise argues that Ms. Ceballos’ Cross-Complaint depends upon
finding that it is liable to Plaintiff, so if found not liable, it would become moot. 1st Stryke states
allowing the Cross-Complaint to proceed during the liability phase would unnecessarily introduce
additional issues concerning allocation of fault and contractual or equitable indemnity before
liability has even been determined. It argues that such evidence could prejudice 1st Stryke by
implicitly suggesting fault to the jury.

Defendant 1st Stryke lastly argues that bifurcation would not prejudice Plaintiff, but it
would significantly prejudice it if it were not granted. 1st Stryke states if liability and damages are
1 It is noted on reply that 1st Stryke changed these estimates: 8 to 10 days for phase one and 5 to 6 days
for phase two. (Supplemental Torello Decl., at ¶ 9.)
not bifurcated as requested, Plaintiff will likely focus all her attention on photos of her in the
hospital and testimony about her current medical condition and her alleged permanent disability
to distract the jury from the lack of admissible evidence of exposure. 1st Stryke states there is a
significant risk that allowing damages testimony to be combined with testimony on liability will
necessitate undue consumption of time and create substantial danger of undue prejudice, of
confusing issues, or of misleading the jury. It further argues that a jury could confuse damages
evidence with liability and potentially find in favor of Plaintiff based purely on damages testimony
when Plaintiff has not been able to meet her burden of proof of establishing liability.
In her opposition, Plaintiff asserts that 1st Stryke did not prove that bifurcation is justified
in this case. Plaintiff argues that bifurcating this trial would be inefficient and costly, not to mention
the facts for both liability and damages are intertwined and arise out of the same set of facts.
Plaintiff states that the presentation of evidence would also confuse jurors by artificially separating
liability from damages.

Plaintiff contends she will need to testify at the trial’s first phase and the trial’s second
phase as well as her family members. She believes Defendants and the City of Ontario’s employee
will only testify in the first phase. However, Plaintiff believes her treating physicians and her
experts would need to testify in both phases. (Declaration of Steven W. Martin, Esq., at ¶ 5, Exh. 3 at pp. 2-3.)
Plaintiff challenges 1st Stryke’s estimates for the trial phases. Plaintiff does not believe the
list of eighteen individuals will take three to five days. She also states that at least six of those
individuals would need to be called back for the portion of trial concerning damages, which is a
waste of their time and the Court’s time. Plaintiff also states that asking these witnesses and experts
to limit their testimony to liability first and damages second will be difficult for them to do and
will confuse a jury. For example, Plaintiff represents that her treating medical providers will be
called to testify as to the issue of liability (the source or sources of poison), causation, and damages,
and it will be burdensome, if not impractical, to require them to appear on two separate occasions.
Plaintiff also states that it will be nearly impossible for the initial medical providers to not talk
about damages when testifying regarding liability, as the way they determined Plaintiff was
poisoned was based on her symptoms and responses to various forms of treatment. Plaintiff further
states that her family members face a significant burden, as several of them live outside the county,
and all have struggled to make time for depositions due to work and caregiving responsibilities.
Plaintiff states asking them to miss work, arrange care, and travel to court twice is both inefficient
and inequitable. Also, Plaintiff expresses that requiring her to testify about the circumstances of
the pesticide exposure while excluding any reference to the harm she suffered deprives jurors of
essential context. Plaintiff thus argues that rather than streamlining trial, bifurcation could extend
it – requiring duplicative witness preparation, courtroom appearances, and judicial oversight.
Plaintiff furthermore states that the opportunity for settlement has passed and contends the
notion that bifurcation will promote settlement is speculative and inaccurate. Plaintiff has already
made every reasonable effort to resolve this case, but Defendants have declined to settle.
As to the differences between 1st Stryke and Ms. Ceballos, Plaintiff states the
circumstances of the injury all stem from the same incident. Plaintiff also argues that bifurcating
trial will certainly cause jury confusion and will likely make the claims against both Defendants
more difficult to understand, as they will be stripped of essential context. 1st Stryke was hired by
Ms. Ceballos and performed a nondelegable duty.

Plaintiff argues that juries are routinely called upon to hear emotionally compelling
evidence, including in cases involving catastrophic injury, wrongful death, and other serious
harms. Plaintiff states the justice system entrusts juries with the ability to follow instructions and
render verdicts based on facts and law – not emotion. And Plaintiff states that her exposure to toxic
pesticides, her resulting injuries, and the knowledge and conduct of both Defendants are part of a
single, cohesive narrative that is most efficiently and fairly tried as a whole. Plaintiff claims that
bifurcation will prejudice her for the reasons already stated above including, time, costs, and the
complexities created by trying a case in two distinct contexts.
In the reply, Defendant 1st Stryke disagrees with Plaintiff that liability and damages are
“intertwined” because the critical question is not whether Plaintiff experienced symptoms but
rather whether 1st Stryke caused those symptoms through exposure to organophosphate pesticide
during the October 15, 2019, service. 1st Stryke states that question turns on the products used,
whether organophosphates were present, whether such substance could have caused symptoms
eight days later, and whether Plaintiff’s diagnosis is scientifically supported. It states these issues
are distinct from the extent of Plaintiff’s alleged injuries.
Defendant 1st Stryke further argues that bifurcation can reduce trial time and may entirely
negate the need for a second phase if there is no liability.
Defendant 1st Stryke further argues that the six witnesses that would return for the second
phase are not only minimal but also involve distinct and non-duplicative subject matter. It also
suggests that remote testimony options can alleviate travel burdens for out-of-country witnesses.
Defendant 1st Stryke additionally argues the treating physicians at the hospital are not
Plaintiff’s current treating physicians and were involved only during the acute phase of care
immediately following her admission. It states that their role is limited and any causation opinions
they may offer are based on patient history and information relayed by others, including the
assertion that the apartment was “fumigated,” by Plaintiff and/or her family members, which 1st
Stryke argues is factually incorrect. It contends that these providers are not true liability witnesses.
Defendant 1st Stryke further argues that while jurors are presumed to follow instructions,
courts routinely recognize that bifurcation is appropriate to prevent prejudice where emotionally
charged damages evidence may influence liability determination. It states that this case involves
particularly graphic and emotionally charged medical evidence about hospitalization, use of life
support, and permanent disability that could improperly influence the liability determination. It
also states that such evidence carries a substantial risk that jurors may reason backward from the
severity of the alleged injuries to conclude that someone must be responsible.
Defendant 1st Stryke then argues the Cross-Complaint and distinct legal duties strongly
support bifurcation. It states that while Plaintiff argues Ms. Ceballos’ claims arise from the same
“incident,” that does not eliminate the distinct legal and factual issues involved. It states that
bifurcation would allow the jury to focus on the specific causation issue related to 1st Stryke
without being burdened by unrelated legal theories.
VIII. Analysis
Defendant 1st Stryke has not shown that bifurcation of liability and damages would
expediate and simplify the presentation of evidence. (Foreman & Clark Corp., supra, 3 Cal.3d
875, 888.) Nor has it shown that such bifurcation would further convenience or promote
expedition and economy. (Code Civ. Proc., § 1048, subd. (b).) 1st Stryke has also not shown that
it will be prejudiced by virtue of the severity of the injuries claimed. (Ibid.)
Plaintiff makes the persuasive argument that one trial would expediate and simplify the
presentation of evidence because her exposure to toxic pesticides, her resulting injuries, and the
knowledge and conduct of both Defendants are part of a single, cohesive narrative that is most
efficiently and fairly tried as a whole. For example, Plaintiff alleges against Defendant 1st Stryke
that it “[was] negligent in the fumigation of the PROPERTY, creating a dangerous condition…”
by “failing to adequately warn and/or safely administer pesticides causing Plaintiff to suffer from
Organophosphate poisoning.” (Compl., at ¶¶ 18, 22; Torello Decl., at ¶ 3, Exh. A.) Because of
those allegations, Plaintiff would likely testify at the first phase about her symptoms from the
alleged poisoning since it is what led to her hospitalization and led to her diagnosis; and her
emergency medical providers will likely need to testify about her reason for admission, which was
identified as organophosphate poisoning, altered mental status. (Torello Decl., at ¶ 3, Exh. B.)
Such testimony also relates to Plaintiff’s claimed damages for having to suffer because of the
alleged poisoning and for having to seek medical treatment to treat her alleged poisoning. It then
seems more appropriate to continue into Plaintiff’s damages. In the reply, Defendant 1st Stryke
argues that the critical question is not whether Plaintiff experienced symptoms, but rather whether
1st Stryke caused those symptoms through exposure to organophosphate pesticide. It states the
question turns on the products used, whether organophosphates were present, whether such
substance could have caused symptoms eight days later, and whether Plaintiff’s diagnosis is
scientifically supported. However, the symptoms still need to be addressed. In this case, liability
and damages arise from the same set of facts.

Bifurcation also would not further convenience nor would it be more economical because
Plaintiff, witnesses, and medical providers/experts will have to testify twice and jurors would have
to serve for a longer period of days. Bifurcation would as a result naturally increase the parties’
expenses.

Both parties agree that there would be overlapping witnesses. All the following individuals
would need to return to the second phase of trial: Plaintiff and her family members (Claudia
Mondragon, Patricia Enriquez, Olga Beyers, Omar Traconis, and Jose Traconis). (Martin, Decl.,
at ¶ 5, Exh. A at p. 3; Supplemental Torello Decl., at ¶ 11, Exh. A at p. 1-2.) Plaintiff also states
her treating physicians and experts would need to testify as to the circumstances of Plaintiff’s
exposure to the poison and resulting injuries and impact on Plaintiff’s life, thus bifurcation would
make it difficult to cleanly separate liability from damages and would likely require them to appear
and testify on multiple occasions. (Martin Decl., at ¶ 5, Exh. A at p. 3.) 1st Stryke does not fully
contest this representation of medical providers and experts having to testify in both the liability
and damages phases. It instead argues that the treating providers are not true liability witnesses,
but this does not negate that they would have to testify twice. Bifurcation thus would not further
convenience because several individuals would need to return for the second phase of trial.
The parties also agree the liability trial phase would be longer than the damages trial phase.
Plaintiff estimates 7 to 9 days for the first phase and Defendant 1st Stryke estimates 8 to 10 days
for the first phase; while Plaintiff estimates 6 to 8 days for the second phase and Defendant 1st
Stryke estimates 5 to 6 days for the second phase. (Martin Decl., at ¶ 5, Exh. A at p. 2;
Supplemental Torello Decl., at ¶ 9 & at ¶ 11, Exh. A at p. 5.) Assuming liability is found, in the
best-case scenario it would take 12 days to complete the first and second phase of trial (Plaintiff’s
estimation of 7 days for the first phase of trial and Defendant 1st Stryke’s estimation of 5 days for
the second phase of trial). But, on the other end, it would take 18 days to complete the first and
second phases of trial (Defendant 1st Stryke’s estimation of 10 days for the first phase of trial and
Plaintiff’s estimation of 8 days for the second phase). Plaintiff estimates a single trial would be
less time, specifically 9 to 11 court days. (Martin Decl., at ¶ 5, Exh. A at p. 1.) 1st Stryke estimates
a single trial would be more time than Plaintiff estimates, specifically 13 to 16 days (Supplemental
Torello Decl., at ¶ 9.) However, an estimate of 13 to 16 days is still less than 18 days. Bifurcation
would not foster judicial economy.

Finally, bifurcation is the exception, not the norm. 1st Stryke does not present evidence to
show the trial of liability issues would be straightforward. It seems the parties will dedicate more
time to such issues. Plaintiff does not have such injuries that would override proper jury
instruction. Jurors will be instructed not to consider sympathy as a factor in their determination of
liability. (People v. Sanchez (2001) 26 Cal.4th 834, 852 [“Jurors are presumed able to understand
and correlate instructions and are further presumed to have followed the court’s instructions.
[Citations.]”].)

CONCLUSION
Based on the foregoing, the Court rules as follows:
(1) DENIES Defendant 1st Stryke’s Motion to Bifurcate Trial, and
(2) ORDERS Plaintiff’s counsel to provide notice.

expected.case_title: Marisol Traconis v. 1st Stryke Pest & Termite Control, et al.
